ta-l1d28q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 28 turns to 'image' and announces three articles: what an image is; whether 'image' in God is said essentially or personally; and, if personally, whether it fits only the Son.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e109.summary: The article sets out Hilary's definition, 'an image is the undifferentiated species of the thing to which it is imaged', and gives the first argument against it. An image imitates in external features, but 'species' signifies the intrinsic quiddity.
claims: Image concerns externals; species is intrinsic.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e115.summary: Second argument. An image properly is what imitates another, but the undifferentiated species of two is not what imitates but that in which imitation is found, so an image should be called 'having a species', not 'a species'.
claims: The image has a species rather than being one.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e118.summary: Third argument. There can be no lack of difference between things infinitely distant, yet the creature is the image of God, from whom it is infinitely distant.
claims: Creature and God are infinitely distant.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e122.summary: Fourth argument. The definition is circular, defining the image by the thing imaged, which can only be defined by the image.
claims: Image and imaged are mutually defined.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e125.summary: Fifth argument. Equality and likeness belong to the concept of image, as Hilary's other definition shows ('an undivided and united likeness of a thing, to equal the thing'), and nothing about them is in this definition.
claims: Image requires equality and likeness.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e131.summary: Thomas's determination. The concept of image consists in imitation, whence the name, 'imago' as 'imitago'. In imitation there is that in which it occurs and the things imitating each other. That in respect of which there is imitation is a quality, or a form signified as quality, so likeness belongs to an image. This is not enough: there must be some equalling in that quality, either in quality or in proportion, as a small image has the same proportion of parts as the large thing, so 'equalling' is in the definition. The quality must also be an express and proximate sign of the nature and species: one who imitates another in whiteness is not his image, but one who imitates in figure is, since figure is the proximate sign of species, as different species of animals have different figures. On the side of the imitating things there is the relation of equality and likeness founded in the one in which they imitate, and further an order: what is later, made to another's likeness, is the image, and what is prior, to whose likeness the other is made, is the exemplar, though one is loosely put for the other. So Hilary signifies the order and relation of the imitating things by 'of the thing to which it is imaged' and that in which imitation occurs by 'undifferentiated species'.
claims: Image consists in imitation in a quality that is an express sign of nature, with equality and an order to an exemplar.
Hilary's definition expresses both the order (to the exemplar) and that in which imitation occurs (undifferentiated species).

ta-l1d28q2-d1e140.summary: Reply to the first argument. The concept of image lies not in imitating any externals but those that are in some way signs of species and nature, which is why Hilary said 'species' rather than 'quality'.
claims: Image imitates signs of species.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e143.summary: Reply to the second argument. The definition is given through the cause: properly the image is not the species in which imitation occurs, but the lack of difference in species is why it is called an image. Or both the imitating thing and that in which imitation occurs can be called image, though the latter less properly, and Hilary defines it so.
claims: The definition is causal, or 'image' is said of the species less properly.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e146.summary: Reply to the third argument. Something attains the concept of image as far as it attains lack of difference; insofar as it differs it is not an image. There are grades of image. Imperfectly, something is called an image when it has something like the quality designating another's nature, though not the nature, as a stone has a man's figure, and so God's image is in creatures, like the king's image on a coin (Augustine). More perfectly, when the nature in species underlies the quality designating it, as a father's image in his son, alike in figure and in the nature figure signifies. Most perfectly, when the numerically same form and nature are in the imitator and the imitated, and so the Son is the most perfect image of the Father, since all divine attributes, signified as qualities, are in him with the nature itself, not only in species but in numerical unity.
claims: Image has three grades: likeness without nature, likeness with specific nature, and numerically the same nature.
The Son is the most perfect image of the Father, having numerically the same nature.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e150.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'Of the thing to which it is imaged' is a circumlocution for 'exemplar', standing for one word, and is fittingly placed in the definition of image, as the prior in the definition of the posterior, not conversely; the exemplar is prior to the image, so there is no circle.
claims: The exemplar is prior and defines the image, without circularity.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e156.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Undifferentiated species' includes the likeness and equality required for an image, so the two definitions come to the same.
claims: Hilary's two definitions are equivalent.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e168.summary: First argument that 'image' is not said essentially. Augustine (Dist. 27) says nothing is more absurd than an image said with respect to itself, and essential names are said with respect to themselves.
claims: An image is not said ad se.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e171.summary: Second argument. Image implies order, and in God the only order is of origin, and nothing implying origin is said essentially.
claims: Image implies order of origin.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e174.summary: Third argument. The distinction of persons cannot be proved from absolutes or essentials, since natural reason reaches the essentials of the Trinity but not the distinction of persons, yet the distinction of persons was proved from the concept of image (Dist. 2).
claims: Image was used to prove distinction of persons.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e178.summary: Sed contra from Augustine and Hilary in the text.
claims: Augustine and Hilary use 'image' essentially.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e181.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Image' can mean what imitates another or that in which imitation occurs. Taken properly, as what imitates another, the divine essence cannot be called image but exemplar, whose image is the creature, since an image presupposes an order to a principle and the essence has none; but a person can be called the image of another, since a person presupposes another by order of nature. So in its proper sense, said of God, 'image' is always personal. Taken as that in which imitation occurs, the divine nature is an image, since in it there are two imitations: of person by person, as the Son imitates the Father in the nature he has from him, and of creature by Creator, imperfectly by some likeness of his goodness. For the first, 'image' signifies the essence directly and the persons obliquely, meaning the divine nature of the persons who imitate each other in it, and so Hilary took it, proving from it both the unity of essence and the distinction of persons. For the second, 'image' signifies the divine essence and connotes relation to the creature imitating it, and so Augustine took it, proving from it only the unity of essence.
claims: Properly, as what imitates, 'image' is always personal in God; the essence is exemplar.
As that in which imitation occurs, the divine nature is an image, between the persons (Hilary) or with respect to creatures (Augustine).

ta-l1d28q2-d1e196.summary: First argument that the Holy Spirit can be called image: Damascene says the Spirit is the image of the Son.
claims: Damascene calls the Spirit image of the Son.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e199.summary: Second argument. As the Son imitates the Father, alike in everything, so does the Spirit, which is what the perfect concept of image requires.
claims: The Spirit is wholly like the Father.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e202.summary: Third argument, against the reply that the Spirit is not like the Father in all things by the character of his procession, as the Son is as begotten. The Spirit's procession is not only of love but of divine love, which as such is in the fullness of the same nature.
claims: Divine love proceeds in fullness of nature.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e206.summary: Fourth argument. The Spirit is said absolutely to be equal, like, and connatural to the Father, though not by the character of his procession absolutely, and these constitute the perfect concept of image.
claims: Equality, likeness, connaturality make an image.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e209.summary: Sed contra. Hilary says eternity is in the Father, species in the Image, and use in the Gift, so as Gift is proper to the Spirit, Image is proper to the Son, as Augustine also holds (Dist. 27).
claims: Image is proper to the Son as Gift to the Spirit.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e212.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Image' said personally fits only the Son. Some say that since image implies imitation in externals, and notional features are like externals in God, the Son is the Father's image because he imitates him in a notion, common spiration, which the Spirit shares with no one. This fails, since notional features are no more like externals than essential ones, except those following substance (Damascene), so imitation in those would also make an image; and since likeness and equality are not found by relations of origin (Augustine, Dist. 20), while image requires them. Others say one thing cannot have several immediate images except divided by matter, nor can one thing be the image of several, so since the Son is the Father's image the Spirit cannot be, nor of Father and Son. This fails too, since the Spirit relates to Father and Son as one principle and could be their image as such, as man is the image of the whole Trinity, and there is no more reason why one cannot have several images than several like or equal things, which in God occurs by distinction of relations, not division of matter. So, with others: though the conceptual diversity of attributes does not suffice for a real distinction of processions, it suffices for their different notions (Dist. 13). Though the Spirit receives the nature by his procession, since it is not by way of nature it is not generation, and so he is not called Son. Likewise the Son is an image by the character of his procession, both as Son, having the Father's nature, and as Word, a likeness in the intellect of the thing understood (Dist. 27). The Spirit does not have this by the character of his procession, proceeding as love, so as he is not called Son, though he receives the Father's nature, neither is he called image, though he is like the Father.
claims: Personally, only the Son is Image, by the character of his procession as Son and Word.
The Spirit, proceeding as love, is not Image, as he is not Son, though like the Father and receiving his nature.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e215.summary: Reply to the first argument. Damascene takes 'image' broadly for any likeness.
claims: Damascene uses 'image' broadly.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e218.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although the Spirit imitates the Father, he does not by the character of his procession have it that he is called image, so he is not called image, as he is not called Son.
claims: The Spirit's likeness is not from the character of his procession.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e221.summary: Reply to the third argument. Real identity in God does not prejudice the conceptual distinction among the attributes, which is true, so though divine wisdom is the essence, the proper concept of wisdom remains beyond that of essence, and likewise will beyond nature and intellect. So the processions by will, by intellect, and by nature remain distinct at least conceptually, and diversity of concepts causes diversity of names, which would never coincide unless their concepts were founded in the same thing. Since procession by will and procession by nature do not belong to the same person in God, the names showing the proper characters of the processions do not follow one another either.
claims: Conceptual distinctions of attributes ground distinct names for the processions.
Procession by will and by nature belong to different persons, so their names do not coincide.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e225.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Although the name 'image' was imposed from equality and likeness, it was imposed to signify a thing to which likeness and equality belong from its mode of production, so something need not be called image absolutely just because it is like and equal, unless it has this from its mode of procession.
claims: 'Image' signifies likeness from mode of production.

ta-l1d28q2-d1e235.summary: An expositio textus. (1) On whether only the Father should be called 'not begotten', each opinion says something true: taken as absolute negation, 'not begotten' does not fit only the Father and is not the same as 'unbegotten', which implies negation by way of privation; taken as negation in the genus of principle, it is the same as 'unbegotten' and fits only the Father. (2) 'It is one thing for the Father to be (patrem esse), another for the Son' changes meaning when transposed. 'Esse' signifies either the truth of a composition or the act of essence. When 'esse' is the predicate of the dictum ('aliud est patrem esse'), it signifies the being that is (as the text reads) an 'accident' of the essence, and the statement is false, since as there is one essence of the three there is one being. When 'patrem' is predicated in the dictum ('aliud est esse patrem'), it signifies the truth of composition, and the Father is Father by that by which it is true to call him Father, paternity, not essence. Since God is called Father by paternity and Son by filiation, it is granted that it is one thing to be Father and another to be Son, with 'aliud' meaning otherness of notion, not of essence.
claims: 'Not begotten' as negation in the genus of principle equals 'unbegotten'.
'Esse' as act of essence is one in the three; 'esse' as truth of composition differs by notion.
concepts: esse as truth of composition vs. act of essence

ta-l1d28q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces three articles on 'image': its definition, whether it is said essentially or personally, and whether personally it fits only the Son.

ta-l1d28q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 defends Hilary's definition of image. Image consists in imitation in a quality that is an express sign of the nature, with equality and an order to an exemplar, which Hilary expresses by 'undifferentiated species' and 'of the thing to which it is imaged'. Image has three grades: likeness without nature (God's image in creatures), likeness with specific nature (a father in his son), and numerically the same nature, which makes the Son the Father's most perfect image. The exemplar is prior, so there is no circle.
claims: Image is imitation in a sign of nature, with equality and order to an exemplar.
The Son is the most perfect image, sharing numerically the same nature.

ta-l1d28q2-Dd1e160.summary: Article 2 holds that 'image', taken properly as what imitates another, is always personal in God, since the essence has no principle and is exemplar, not image. Taken as that in which imitation occurs, the divine nature can be called image, either between the persons (Hilary, proving unity and distinction) or with respect to creatures (Augustine, proving unity only).
claims: Properly, 'image' is personal in God.
As that in which imitation occurs, 'image' can be essential.

ta-l1d28q2-Dd1e188.summary: Article 3 holds that 'image' said personally fits only the Son, rejecting explanations from notional imitation and from the impossibility of several images. The Son is image by the character of his procession, as Son and as Word, while the Spirit, proceeding as love, is not image, just as he is not Son, though he is like the Father. Conceptual distinctions of attributes ground distinct names for the processions, and 'image' signifies likeness from mode of production.
claims: Only the Son is the personal Image, by the character of his procession.

ta-l1d28q2-Dd1e230.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 28 reconciles opinions on 'not begotten' by distinguishing absolute negation from negation in the genus of principle. It explains that 'esse' as act of essence is one in the persons, while 'esse' as truth of composition differs by notion.
claims: 'Not begotten' in the genus of principle equals 'unbegotten'.
Being as act of essence is one in the persons.

ta-l1d28q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 28 treats 'image'. Article 1 defines image as imitation in an express sign of nature, with equality and an order to an exemplar, distinguishing three grades and making the Son the most perfect image as sharing numerically the same nature. Article 2 holds that properly 'image' is personal in God, the essence being exemplar, though the nature can be called image as that in which imitation occurs. Article 3 holds that only the Son is the personal Image, by his procession as Son and Word, while the Spirit, proceeding as love, is not.
claims: Image is imitation with equality and order to an exemplar; the Son is the perfect image.
Properly 'image' is personal and belongs to the Son alone.
